Grammar

Faber's grammar is written down as a list of rules, which the compiler calls productions. Each rule says how one piece of the language is built from smaller pieces: a loop from a keyword, a binding and a block, a block from statements. You do not need to read the rules to write Faber. The cheat sheet and the language pages teach every form by example; this section is for looking up which words belong to which part of the language.

The 258 rules are grouped into the families below. Each family page lists the words you write in that part of the language and links each one to its term page.

Production families#

FamilyWhat it covers
Programs, regions & importsThe shape of a source file: optional frontmatter, the optional module region, the top-level statement spine, imports, and the program entry points and test suites.
Declarations & bindingsBindings, functions, generic parameters, closures, classes, and the fields and methods a class holds.
Annotations & directivesThe @ annotation family: the generic shape, the kernel (@ kernel), compiler-lane (@ radix), and capability (@ call) directives.
Types & contractsType syntax and the declarations built on it: interfaces, type aliases, enums, tagged unions, and relational schemas.
Statements & control flowStatements and control flow: conditionals, loops, switch and match, guards, extraction, loop and function transfer, and the diagnostic statements.
Expressions & operatorsExpressions and the operator stack, from the assignment root down through the precedence ladder to calls, literals, and the collection and JSON forms.
Patterns & destructuringPatterns and destructuring: the atoms a match arm accepts, type and alias patterns, and the object and array destructuring forms.
Error channelThe error channel: throwing, guarded throws, and the local catch handler that recovers an error into a value.
Lexical structure & glyphsThe terminal tokens the lexer produces: identifiers, numbers, strings, width markers, and the frontmatter delimiter.

Formal grammar#

The rules themselves are the parser's own definition of valid syntax. They are written for models and tools, in the English reader spellings, and live on one page: every production, with the shorter forms the agent pages use. The target matrix is the authority on whether a given target supports a form. Latin stays the compiler's canonical form, and faber explain <term> prints a mapping from the compiler itself.
